title: Sponsor and project manager: who does what on the business case
blurb: Tell apart the sponsor's ownership of the business case from the project manager's contribution to it.
question: A hospital's director of estates is sponsoring a new car park barrier system. She asks the project manager to 'write the business case and own it from now on'. What should each of them actually be doing on the business case?

teach.h: The sponsor owns it, the PM contributes
teach.body: The business case belongs to the sponsor: the senior individual accountable for the investment. The sponsor develops and approves it, secures the funding, keeps it valid and is accountable for the benefits it promises. The project manager supports and contributes: estimates of time, cost and resources, delivery planning, risks and feasibility, and help keeping it up to date and aligned with the project.

teach.caption: Think 'owner and adviser': the sponsor makes the case and answers for it; the PM makes sure it can actually be delivered.

teach.h: Why the sponsor, not the PM?
teach.body: The investment is the organisation's, so a senior person must answer for it. The sponsor can see the strategic need, has authority to commit funds and will still be around when benefits arrive, often after the project has closed and the PM has moved on. The PM is closest to the delivery detail, which is exactly what the case needs to be realistic.

teach.h: Who brings what to the business case
Working together through the life cycle

steps.label: Concept
steps.sub: Sponsor sets out the need and options; PM gives early estimates

steps.label: Definition
steps.sub: PM supplies detailed estimates and plans; sponsor refines the case

steps.label: Decision gate
steps.sub: Sponsor presents and approves; PM reports delivery feasibility

steps.label: Deployment
steps.sub: PM flags changes to cost, time or risk; sponsor keeps it valid

steps.label: After closure
steps.sub: Sponsor remains accountable for realising benefits

teach.body: Fiona, Director of Estates, sponsors a new barrier and payment system. She writes the case for change (patients can't park, income is lost) and secures funding. Raj, the PM, estimates installation time, cost and staffing for each option and flags the risk of disruption to A&E access. Mid-deployment, supplier prices rise. Raj reports the new figures; Fiona decides whether the case still stands.

rows.label: Helps keep the case up to date

teach.note: Both care about the case staying valid: the sponsor is accountable for it, the PM feeds in the facts.

teach.h: Who does what, step by step
head: Activity
Sponsor
Project manager
rows: Keep the case valid in delivery

teach.text: Classic distractors: 'the project manager owns the business case', 'the PM approves the funding', 'the PMO or finance team writes and owns it'. The SPONSOR owns the business case. The PM CONTRIBUTES to it, mainly with estimates, plans and delivery risks.

items: Sponsor: owns the business case, develops and approves it, secures funding, keeps it valid, accountable for benefits.
Project manager: supports and contributes estimates of time, cost and resources, delivery planning, risks and feasibility.
The PM helps keep the case up to date; the sponsor decides whether it is still justified.
Benefits accountability stays with the sponsor, often beyond project closure.

summary: You can now explain that the sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for it and its benefits, while the project manager contributes the estimates, delivery planning and risk information that make it realistic. You can also describe how they work together to keep it valid through the life cycle.

A.q: Who owns the business case for a project?
options: The project manager
The project sponsor
The governance board
The project office
A.why: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for it and for the benefits it promises.

whyNot.0: The project manager contributes to the business case but does not own it.
whyNot.2: The board, usually chaired by the sponsor, reviews it at gates; ownership sits with the sponsor.
whyNot.3: A PMO supports projects with standards and information; it does not own the case.

A.q: Which of the following is a typical project manager contribution to the business case?
options: Final approval of the funding
Accountability for the benefits
Estimates of time, cost and resources
Deciding the organisation's strategy
A.why: The PM supports the case with delivery information such as time, cost and resource estimates.

whyNot.0: Approving and securing funding is the sponsor's role.
whyNot.1: The sponsor is accountable for benefits realisation.
whyNot.3: Strategy is set by senior management; the sponsor checks the project's fit with it.

A.q: Why is the sponsor, rather than the project manager, accountable for the business case?
options: The sponsor answers for the investment and its benefits
The sponsor produces all the detailed cost estimates
The sponsor manages the project team day to day
The sponsor writes the technical specification
A.why: The sponsor is the senior individual accountable for the investment delivering its intended benefits to the organisation.

whyNot.1: Detailed estimates come from the PM and team.
whyNot.2: Day-to-day management is the project manager's job.
whyNot.3: Technical specifications are produced by specialists, not the sponsor.

B.q: Complete the statement: the sponsor ______ the business case and the project manager ______ to it.
options: writes ... agrees
approves ... owns
contributes ... owns
owns ... contributes
B.why: The sponsor owns the business case; the project manager contributes estimates, plans and delivery risks.

whyNot.0: The PM does not hold the agreeing or approving role; that is the sponsor.
whyNot.1: The PM does not own the business case.

B.q: During deployment, the project manager learns that supplier price rises will add 20% to the cost. What should the PM do about the business case?
options: Give the sponsor updated estimates so the case can be reviewed
Rewrite and re-approve the business case on their own authority
Wait until handover before mentioning the higher cost to anyone
Quietly reduce the scope so the original case still holds true
B.why: The PM helps keep the case up to date by reporting changes; the sponsor, as owner, decides whether it remains valid.

whyNot.1: Approving the business case is for the sponsor, not the PM.
whyNot.2: Delay hides information the sponsor needs to keep the case valid.
whyNot.3: Changing scope needs change control and the sponsor's decision, not a quiet fix.

B.q: Which TWO of the following are the sponsor's responsibilities for the business case? 1. Securing the funding 2. Estimating activity durations 3. Keeping the case valid 4. Drafting the detailed schedule
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: The sponsor secures funding and is accountable for keeping the business case valid.

whyNot.0: Estimating durations is a PM and team contribution.
whyNot.3: Drafting the schedule is the PM's work.

C.q: A busy sponsor tells a new project manager: 'You own the business case now.' What is the main problem with this?
options: The PM is not allowed to read the business case
Ownership should stay with the accountable sponsor
Handing it over automatically cancels the funding
The business case only matters before approval
C.why: The sponsor remains accountable for the business case and its benefits; the PM supports it but should not take ownership.

whyNot.0: The PM uses and contributes to the business case, so they must see it.
whyNot.2: Funding is not cancelled automatically; the problem is misplaced accountability.
whyNot.3: The case stays live throughout the project and into benefits realisation.

C.q: At a decision gate, which pairing best describes each role's part in the business case review?
options: PM approves the case; sponsor provides estimates
PMO decides; sponsor and PM both simply observe
Sponsor presents and decides; PM reports feasibility
Team presents the case; PM approves continuation
C.why: The sponsor, as owner, champions the case and makes or seeks the go / no-go decision; the PM reports on delivery progress and feasibility.

whyNot.1: A PMO supports governance but does not make the gate decision.
whyNot.3: Neither the team nor the PM approves continuation; that sits with the sponsor and board.

C.q: Which statement about the project manager's role in the business case is NOT correct?
options: They provide estimates for the options
They help keep the case up to date
They supply delivery risks and feasibility
They approve the investment decision
C.why: Approving the investment is the sponsor's (or board's) decision; the PM contributes information to it.

whyNot.0: Providing estimates for options is a core PM contribution.
whyNot.1: The PM helps keep the case current by reporting changes.
whyNot.2: Delivery risks and feasibility input are part of the PM's contribution.

reteach.title: Think of a house extension
reteach.question: You are paying for a kitchen extension and have hired a builder to run the job. Who should own the decision that it's worth the money?

blocks.body: You, the homeowner, are the sponsor. It is your money, your reason for wanting more space, and you will live with the result for years. The builder is the project manager. They price the work, say how long it will take and warn you about risks like drainage or planning permission. You decide whether it is still worth it. You would never let the builder decide to spend your savings.

blocks.h: Who does what on the extension

blocks.text: If the builder finds a problem that pushes the price up, they tell you; you decide whether to carry on. Same on a project: the PM reports, the sponsor decides.

explain.body: The sponsor is accountable for the business case: developing and approving it, securing funding and championing the investment at senior level.

test.q: Which of the following is the sponsor's job in developing the business case?
options: Securing the funding for the work
Breaking the work into packages
Estimating each activity's length
Running the team's daily meetings
test.why: Securing funding for the investment is part of the sponsor's ownership of the business case.

whyNot.1: Work breakdown is a PM and team planning task.
whyNot.2: Activity estimates come from the PM and team.
whyNot.3: Running the team day to day is the PM's role.

explain.body: The project manager makes the case realistic by supplying estimates of time, cost and resources, a view of how it could be delivered, and the delivery risks and feasibility of each option.

test.q: The project manager's estimates feed most directly into which parts of the business case?
options: Strategic context and need
Benefits ownership and review
Costs and timescales
Organisational strategy
test.why: Time, cost and resource estimates shape the costs and timescales in the business case.

whyNot.0: The strategic context and need are set out by the sponsor.
whyNot.1: Benefits ownership sits with the sponsor and business.
whyNot.3: Strategy is set by the organisation's leadership, not by project estimates.

explain.body: During delivery, the PM monitors cost, time and risk and reports changes that affect the case. The sponsor, as owner, decides whether it is still justified, which might mean changing course or stopping.

test.q: During deployment, what is the project manager's main part in keeping the business case valid?
options: Reporting changes in cost, time or risk
Approving revisions to the business case
Deciding alone whether the project stops
Securing extra funding from the board
test.why: The PM keeps the case aligned by reporting changes that affect it; the sponsor decides what to do.

whyNot.1: Approving revisions is the sponsor's role as owner.
whyNot.2: Stopping the project is a sponsor or governance decision.
whyNot.3: Securing funding is the sponsor's responsibility.

explain.body: Many benefits are realised after the project closes. The PM's role ends at closure, but the sponsor stays accountable for making sure the promised benefits are realised.

test.q: Which statement about benefits accountability is correct?
options: The PM is accountable until all benefits arrive
End users own the business case after handover
The PMO takes accountability once work closes
The sponsor is accountable, often after closure
test.why: The sponsor is accountable for benefits realisation, which often continues after the project has closed.

whyNot.0: The PM's role normally ends at closure, before many benefits arrive.
whyNot.1: End users help realise benefits, but the sponsor owns the case.
whyNot.2: A PMO supports and reports; it does not take on benefits accountability.
